c: , is a visual design aesthetic that was popularized in the late 2000s and remained prominent through the mid 2010s. It is characterized by old-timey Americana imagery, badges and seals, hand-lettered and ornamental typography, decorative borders, and vintage commercial ephemera.
The name "Genericana" is a portmanteau of the words "generic" and "Americana," and was coined by
researcher tranquility2099. Its primary alternate title, "Contemporary-Conformist," comes from a series of satirical blog posts by "Carles," the anonymous creator of
and its successor, Carles.Buzz, both of which are no longer in operation. Carles' work, though parodic, is the source for most of the foundational research of the Genericana aesthetic.
Genericana is most closely tied to the

subculture that existed alongside the styles' conception and rise, from the late 2000s to the mid 2010s. Many brands and businesses at the time utilized this design style to make themselves feel "artisanal" and "authentic," relying on vintage-style and seemingly hand-drawn graphics to appear to be traditional and hand-crafted. In a 2020 qualitative study published in the International Journal of Design, titled "Hip and Authentic. Defining Neo-Retro Style in Package Design," researchers sought to understand the base characteristics of Genericana (referred to as "Neo-Retro" in the study), as well as the values associated with the style, examining how closely the public perception of Genericana connnects to the values of the Hipster subculture. Their study found that most people did associate Genericana with "authenticity," "retro," "craftsmanship," and "originality," directly corresponding to many of the values held within the Hipster community.

Further analysis of the style arose from Hipster Runoff, a now-defunct parody blog launched in 2007 that provided humorous commentary on alternative music, contemporary subcultures, and breaking news of the time. Dubbing the style (and the people drawn to it) as "Contemporary Conformist," blog-writer Carles poked fun at its frivolity and tackiness, saying "...the Contemporary Conformist couple uses their ‘design aesthetic’ to create a ‘natural’ urban vintage rural look using their ‘great taste’ that is completely in line with contemporary conformism." Carles often attacked the Contemporary Conformists' need for things to feel worldly, artisanal, and authentic, explaining in his original post: "The Contemporary Conformist is grounded in nothing. They have no sense of the world. They are not traveled. They do not actually ‘know’ cuisine. They only have a collection of consumer experiences." No aspect of Hipster life was safe from his critique -- from Genericana and
Sometime in the 2020s, the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute (also known as CARI) officially identified and titled this aesthetic "Genericana."
The study "Hip and Authentic. Defining Neo-Retro Style in Package Design" identified a few key components of the Genericana style:
Packaging with texture and material imperfections
The usage of organic and raw materials such as wood, leather, brick, brown paper and cardboard
An intentional mixture of different typefaces from different families
Illustrations that seem hand-drawn or products of engraving or woodcutting
Swashes, flourishes, double strokes, and other ornamental patterns
Graphical textures, meant to "roughen up" vector graphics and make them seem handmade.
Genericana also embraces the usage of
Edison bulbs, badges, crests and stamps, folk illustrations, and Victorian ornamentary pieces such as flourishes, curls, and ornate typography
used decoratively to make the branding feel authentic.
